standard.title: Environmental change: causes, effects and management strategies
standard.description: causes and effects of a change in an identified environment at a local, national or global scale, and strategies to manage sustainability
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand human-induced environmental changes and sustainability (AC9HG10K01), environmental world views (AC9HG10K02), and First Nations custodial approaches (AC9HG10K03). They have engaged with sustainability strategies for biomes (AC9HG9K04) and urban places (AC9HG8K09), providing a prior framework for evaluating management strategies.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the causes and effects of a change in an identified environment and propose and compare strategies to manage sustainability, drawing on environmental, economic and social criteria and considering trade-offs and the perspectives of different stakeholders.

nodes.label: Identifying context and describing causes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify a specific environmental change context, describe its causes, and explain the impacts on the sustainability of the environment's functions.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the causes of environmental change in one identified context and explain impacts on at least one environmental function (resource, service or spiritual).
nodes.typical_width: Describe the causes of environmental change in a studied context across local, national or global scale as appropriate; explain impacts on multiple environmental functions including resource provision, ecological services, and cultural or spiritual value.
wider: Investigate a complex multi-causal environmental change case (e.g. Murray-Darling Basin water stress, Great Barrier Reef bleaching) tracing the interaction of natural and human factors at different scales

Analyse how scale of study changes the apparent causes and effects — for example, localised agricultural runoff vs national water policy vs global climate change as causes of the same environmental change
Examine an environmental change case in a developing country context and compare the causes and affected environmental functions with an equivalent change in Australia
nodes.hinge_reason: Without an accurate and specific account of causes and affected environmental functions in their studied context, students cannot evaluate whether proposed strategies actually address the right problem — the entire evaluation chain (nodes 2–3) depends on the cause-effect analysis being correct.

response_modes.reason: Students often list causes without tracing causal mechanisms or explaining which environmental functions are affected and how. Scaffolding the cause → mechanism → function impact chain explicitly prevents superficial cause listing.

success_criteria: Students identify a specific environmental change context and describe at least two causes with their mechanisms
Students explain the impact of the change on at least one environmental function using correct geographical terminology

nodes.label: World views and strategy development
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise how people's world views influence how management strategies are developed and implemented, and identify who is involved in strategy decision-making.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two stakeholder groups involved in developing a management strategy for the studied context and explain how their world views influence the strategies they support.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how Traditional Owners, communities, developers, governments and NGOs use environmental, economic and social criteria when making decisions; show how world view (human-centred vs earth-centred) shapes which criteria are prioritised and what trade-offs are accepted.
wider: Analyse a documented governance process (e.g. an environmental impact assessment, a resource management tribunal) to trace how different stakeholder world views are weighted in formal decision-making
Investigate a case where First Nations Traditional Owners' world views and management priorities diverged from government or NGO approaches, examining how the tension was or was not resolved

Compare decision-making criteria for environmental management in two different national governance systems (e.g. Australia vs India) examining how institutional structures encode different world views

response_modes.reason: Students need exposure to multiple stakeholder configurations — not just community vs government — to build a flexible understanding of how world views shape strategy development in different governance contexts.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The intersection of world views and governance processes is substantively rich — real decision-making cases reveal the complexity that cannot be accessed through hypothetical scenarios alone.
success_criteria: Students identify at least two stakeholders involved in developing a management strategy and explain how their different world views influence the strategy they support
Students identify at least one trade-off that decision-makers face and explain how different stakeholders evaluate that trade-off differently

nodes.label: Proposing and comparing management strategies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can propose strategies to manage the effects of environmental change and compare strategies in terms of environmental, economic and social criteria, including cross-national comparison where appropriate.
nodes.minimum_width: Propose at least one management strategy for the studied context and evaluate it against at least one criterion (environmental, economic or social).
nodes.typical_width: Propose and evaluate multiple strategies using environmental, economic and social criteria; compare strategies in Australia with strategies in another country for human-induced environmental change, using stated criteria and acknowledging trade-offs.
wider: Compare three strategy types — environmental (marine reserves, national parks), spatial (corridors, urban planning) and holistic (addressing past and present causes) — evaluating the criteria each type is best suited to address
Evaluate the effectiveness of a real implemented strategy over time using before/after evidence, identifying what was achieved and what remained unresolved
Develop and justify a prioritised strategy recommendation that explicitly addresses the different criteria and trade-offs involved, including acknowledgment of First Nations approaches where relevant

response_modes.reason: This node integrates cause-effect analysis, world view awareness and multi-criteria evaluation into a strategy proposal. The teacher signal is to make the connections explicit: a good strategy proposal flows directly from the cause-effect analysis (Node 1) and accounts for the stakeholder world views identified in Node 2.

Strategy comparison requires applying consistent criteria across cases — students often compare incomparable things (effectiveness vs cost vs acceptability) without acknowledging they are using different criteria. Scaffold the criteria framework before asking for comparison.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Cross-national strategy comparison is explicitly mandated in the descriptor (e.g. waste management Australia vs India, flood management Australia vs China). Students who have compared strategies across multiple national contexts develop a more rigorous evaluative framework.
success_criteria: Students propose at least one management strategy and evaluate it against at least two criteria (environmental, economic, social)
Students explain a trade-off involved in their proposed strategy and acknowledge why different stakeholders may evaluate the trade-off differently
